title: Effects of Computerized Clinical Decision Support Systems on Practitioner Performance and Patient Outcomes: A Systematic Review
authors: Garg AX, Adhikari NKJ, McDonald H, et al.
metadata_verified_via: Full-text PDF copy (Univ. Alberta) + AHRQ PSNet record
objective: Assess effects of computerized CDSS on practitioner performance and patient outcomes
architecture_methods: Systematic review of controlled trials of knowledge-based CDSS (diagnostic, reminder, disease management, drug dosing)
dataset_sample: 100 controlled trials
metrics: Proportion of trials showing improved practitioner performance / patient outcomes
main_findings: Practitioner performance improved in 62/97 trials (64%): diagnostic 4/10 (40%), reminder 16/21 (76%), disease management 23/37 (62%), drug dosing/prescribing 19/29 (66%). Patient outcomes improved in 7/52 trials (13%). Automatic prompting 73% (44/60) vs user-initiated 47% (17/36) success (P=.02). Developer-authored trials 74% (51/69) vs 28% (5/18) (P=.001).
limitations: Vote counting of trial significance; pre-2005 systems; heterogeneous outcomes
relevance: P4/RQ4: developer-evaluation bias; RQ1: process vs outcome gap
supports_or_contradicts: Supports independent evaluation with matched baselines; establishes modest classical CDSS effects
claims_supported: CDSS often improve practitioner performance but rarely demonstrate patient-outcome benefit; developer-run evaluations report more success

title: Improving clinical practice using clinical decision support systems: a systematic review of trials to identify features critical to success
authors: Kawamoto K, Houlihan CA, Balas EA, Lobach DF
metadata_verified_via: AHRQ PSNet record (volume/issue/start page); DOI not confirmed on any page read, so left blank
objective: Identify CDSS features critical to improving clinical practice
architecture_methods: Systematic review of RCTs with feature analysis
dataset_sample: 70 RCTs
metrics: Proportion of trials improving clinical practice; features associated with success
main_findings: CDSS improved clinical practice in nearly 70% of trials. Features independently associated with success: automatic provision as part of workflow; recommendations rather than assessments only; support at time and location of decision making; computer-based.
limitations: Full text not read (PMC captcha); '94% with all features' figure NOT verified; odds ratios not extracted
relevance: Background 2.1; design lessons for integration and actionable output (RQ1)
supports_or_contradicts: Supports actionable, workflow-integrated output design
claims_supported: Workflow integration and actionable recommendations predict CDSS success

title: Computerised clinical decision support systems and absolute improvements in care: meta-analysis of controlled clinical trials
authors: Kwan JL, Lo L, Ferguson J, Goldberg H, Diaz-Martinez JP, Tomlinson G, Grimshaw JM, Shojania KG
metadata_verified_via: BMJ publisher page
objective: Quantify absolute improvements in process of care from CDSS and explore heterogeneity
architecture_methods: Multilevel meta-analysis and meta-regression of RCTs/quasi-RCTs of CDSS embedded in clinical systems; Medline to Aug 2019
dataset_sample: Abstract: 108 studies, 122 trials, 1,203,053 patients, 10,790 providers (Results section states 115 studies / 129 trials - inconsistency in source)
metrics: Absolute % of patients receiving recommended care; clinical endpoint targets
main_findings: Pooled absolute improvement 5.8% (95% CI 4.0-7.6), I2=76%; top quartile 10-62%. Prescribing +4.4%, test ordering +6.8%, documentation +7.1%, vaccination +5.9%. Clinical endpoints (30 trials): median +0.3% (IQR -0.7 to 1.9). Requiring reason for non-adherence +4.8% (0.1-9.6); executable action +4.4% (0.9-7.9); paediatric +13.6% (multivariable); considering alert fatigue +1.7% (NS). Only ~17-19 trials considered alert fatigue.
limitations: Extreme unexplained heterogeneity; sparse clinical outcomes; Medline only; unit-of-analysis errors in 18 of 113 cluster trials
relevance: 2.1 CDSS effectiveness; RQ1 (cost of alert fatigue vs small gains)
supports_or_contradicts: Supports 'modest, variable effect' framing; cautions against over-alerting
claims_supported: CDSS yield small-to-moderate process gains (+5.8 points) with negligible clinical-endpoint gains; improvement is 'largely trial and error'

title: An overview of clinical decision support systems: benefits, risks, and strategies for success
authors: Sutton RT, Pincock D, Baumgart DC, Sadowski DC, Fedorak RN, Kroeker KI

title: Overriding of drug safety alerts in computerized physician order entry
authors: van der Sijs H, Aarts J, Vulto A, Berg M
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association 13(2):138-147
metadata_verified_via: Erasmus University repository record

architecture_methods: Literature review interpreted with Reason's accident-causation model
dataset_sample: 17 papers
metrics: Override rate
main_findings: Drug safety alerts overridden in 49% to 96% of cases; overriding often justified; error-producing conditions include low sensitivity/specificity, unclear content, unnecessary workflow disruption.

title: Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators
authors: Goddard K, Roudsari A, Wyatt JC
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association 19(1):121 (online 16 Jun 2011)
metadata_verified_via: WUSTL journal-club record (PMID 21685142, online date); vol/issue/page from OUP URL path only; DOI not confirmed on any page read, so left blank
objective: Review frequency, mediators and mitigators of automation bias with decision support
architecture_methods: Systematic review
dataset_sample: 13,821 papers retrieved, 74 included
main_findings: Mediators: cognitive style, task-specific experience, trust/confidence, workload, task complexity, time pressure. Mitigators: training, user accountability, on-screen position of advice, updated confidence levels on output, providing information vs recommendation. No numeric effect sizes in abstract.
limitations: Full text inaccessible (Anubis block, OUP server error); no numbers extracted
relevance: 2.1 automation bias; human-oversight design
supports_or_contradicts: Supports non-directive, evidence-showing output; cautions that physician oversight is itself vulnerable
claims_supported: Automation bias is mediated by trust, workload and task complexity; mitigated by design and accountability

title: External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients
authors: Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP, et al.
metadata_verified_via: PMC page (PMID 34152373); page range not verified
objective: Externally validate the Epic Sepsis Model
architecture_methods: Retrospective cohort external validation of proprietary ML CDSS
dataset_sample: Michigan Medicine, 27,697 patients, 38,455 hospitalizations (Dec 2018-Oct 2019); sepsis 7%
metrics: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, alert burden
main_findings: AUC 0.63 (95% CI 0.62-0.64) vs developer-reported 0.76-0.83. At threshold >=6: sensitivity 33%, specificity 83%, PPV 12%. Missed 67% (1,709/2,552) of sepsis cases; alerted on 18% of hospitalizations.

relevance: P4/RQ4: real-data external validation exposes inflated internal metrics
supports_or_contradicts: Supports real-data, independent evaluation
claims_supported: Deployed ML CDSS can underperform developer claims substantially on external real data

title: Can Generalist Foundation Models Outcompete Special-Purpose Tuning? Case Study in Medicine
authors: Nori H, Lee YT, Zhang S, et al. (19 authors; Horvitz E senior)

title: Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for large language model interpretability in medicine
authors: Savage T, Nayak A, Gallo R, Rangan E, Chen JH
metadata_verified_via: Nature publisher PDF
objective: Test whether clinician-style diagnostic reasoning prompts improve LLM accuracy and interpretability

metrics: Accuracy; rationale logic review
main_findings: GPT-4 MedQA: CoT 76%, intuitive 77%, analytic 78%, differential 78%, Bayesian 72% (all NS vs CoT). GPT-3.5: CoT 46%; analytic -6.0% (p=0.001), differential -8.9% (p<0.001). NEJM: GPT-4 CoT 38% vs differential 34%. 65% of incorrect vs 18% of correct GPT-4 rationales had false logic.

title: Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making
authors: Hager P, Jungmann F, Holland R, Bhagat K, Hubrecht I, Knauer M, Vielhauer J, Makowski M, Braren R, Kaissis G, Rueckert D
metadata_verified_via: TUM research portal (this session); full text = accepted manuscript (prior session)

architecture_methods: Single LLM agent iteratively requesting exam/lab/imaging via tools; full-information variant; mitigation by summarization/filtering

main_findings: Autonomous vs full information: Llama 2 Chat 58.8%->45.5%, OASST 67.8%->54.9%, WizardLM 65.1%->53.9%. Worse than physicians (P<0.001). authors: Omar M, Soffer S, Agbareia R, Bragazzi NL, Apakama DU, Horowitz CR, Charney AW, Freeman R, Kummer B, Glicksberg BS, Nadkarni GN, Klang E
published_version_checked: yes (medRxiv 10.1101/2024.10.29.24316368 -> Nature Medicine 2025, per press release)

architecture_methods: Counterfactual label perturbation
dataset_sample: 1,000 ED cases x 32 sociodemographic profiles; >1.7 million outputs
metrics: Triage, testing, treatment, mental-health evaluation recommendations

title: MedFuzz: Exploring the Robustness of Large Language Models in Medical Question Answering
authors: Ness RO, Matton K, Helm H, Zhang S, Bajwa J, Priebe CE, Horvitz E
published_version_checked: no (no venue found in this session)
metadata_verified_via: arXiv HTML v2
objective: Adversarially test robustness of medical QA to assumption-violating rewrites
architecture_methods: Attacker LLM (GPT-4 Turbo) iteratively rewrites MedQA items adding stereotype-appealing patient details; permutation test vs control fuzzes
models_tools: GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4 Turbo, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, OpenBioLLM-70B, Meditron-70B, BioMistral-7B, Medllama3-v20
dataset_sample: 1,181 US MedQA items; up to 5 attacks; 5 replicates; temperature 1.0
metrics: Accuracy after attack; CoT faithfulness
main_findings: GPT-4 and Claude remain near human-comparable accuracy (76.6% human average) after 5 attacks (exact values in Fig. 2 not extracted). For GPT-3.5/GPT-4, ~10-20% of successful attacks had CoT omitting all fuzzed information; most explanations omitted at least one inserted cue.
limitations: Preprint; numbers in figures only; contamination not addressed
relevance: RQ3 wording perturbation; P3 rationale unfaithfulness
supports_or_contradicts: Supports perturbation sensitivity and unfaithful explanations
claims_supported: LLM explanations often omit the inserted detail that changed the answer

title: A statistical framework for evaluating the repeatability and reproducibility of large language models
authors: Shyr C, Ren B, Hsu CY, Yan C, Tinker RJ, Cassini TA, Hamid R, Wright A, Bastarache L, Peterson JF, Malin BA, Xu H
published_version_checked: unclear (PMC12637745 appeared in search but was not opened; journal version not confirmed)
metadata_verified_via: medRxiv full-text PDF
objective: Quantify repeatability and reproducibility of LLM diagnostic outputs
architecture_methods: 100 runs per prompt-case-model; semantic (embedding cosine) and internal (entropy) repeatability/reproducibility metrics; 5 CoT prompts
dataset_sample: 518 USMLE free-response vignettes; 90 UDN rare-disease cases; 912,000 generations (temperature 0.5)
metrics: Semantic/internal repeatability and reproducibility scores
main_findings: Repeatability and reproducibility depend jointly on model, prompt and dataset; differences significant (e.g., GPT-4o-mini semantic repeatability across prompts p<0.001). For GPT-4 on USMLE, repeatability generally did not differ between correct and incorrect diagnoses. No answer-flip proportion reported.
limitations: Preprint; embedding/entropy metrics rather than decision flip rates; fixed temperature
relevance: RQ3: run-to-run inconsistency measurement
supports_or_contradicts: Supports evaluating consistency separately from accuracy
claims_supported: LLM diagnostic output consistency varies with model, prompt and dataset and is distinct from accuracy

title: Large language models propagate race-based medicine

metrics: Qualitative presence of race-based content

title: Large Language Models lack essential metacognition for reliable medical reasoning
authors: Griot M, Hemptinne C, Vanderdonckt J, Yuksel D
metadata_verified_via: RePEc/IDEAS record (prior session)
objective: Assess LLM metacognition and calibration (MetaMedQA)
architecture_methods: MCQ with confidence, missing-answer and unknown-answer tasks
dataset_sample: MetaMedQA
metrics: Accuracy, confidence calibration, unknown recall
main_findings: Models achieved high MCQ accuracy but consistently failed to recognise knowledge limitations, answering confidently when the correct option was absent. Numeric results only from secondary news (not to be cited).
limitations: Abstract only; numbers secondary
relevance: P2 / RQ1: verbalised confidence unreliable for gating
supports_or_contradicts: Argues against confidence-prompt baselines; supports sampling- or rule-based abstention
